criteria.description: Correctly identifies the O(n^2) vs O(nk) computational cost tradeoff.
Correctly explains why nearby pairs are more valuable to check than distant pairs.

solutions.fullSolution: All-pairs connection would need O(n^2) collision-check calls (one of the most expensive parts of PRM construction); restricting to k nearest neighbors reduces this to O(nk). Nearby configurations are far more likely to have a collision-free straight-line connection than distant ones, so most all-pairs value would be wasted on doomed-to-fail distant pairs. Tradeoff: some possible edges can be missed, but a well-connected roadmap only needs enough local edges for graph search to find a path, not every possible direct edge.

Exponent: -sigma*rho^d*n = -1*0.1^2*5 = -0.05, e^-0.05 ~= 0.9512. Prefactor: 2*gamma/rho = 2/0.1 = 20. Bound = 1 - 20*0.9512 ~= 1 - 19.02 ~= -18.02, a vacuous (negative) lower bound. (Independently verified with direct Python computation; rho=1.0 with the same other parameters gives ~0.987 instead.)

criteria.description: Correctly explains that sparse regions are nearest-neighbor to more random samples on average.
Correctly connects this to the self-correcting bias toward unexplored space.

solutions.fullSolution: Sparsely-covered regions are, on average, closer (nearest-neighbor sense) to a larger share of uniformly random target samples than densely-covered regions. So sparse regions get selected as 'nearest neighbor' more often, pulling growth preferentially toward unexplored space, a self-correcting bias. This is why the tree ends up roughly evenly spread without ever computing or targeting uniform coverage explicitly.

criteria.description: Correctly justifies via amortized precomputation over many queries in a fixed environment.

solutions.fullSolution: PRM: precomputation cost (building the roadmap once) is paid once and amortized over every subsequent query; RRT would redo its tree-growing work from scratch for every new (start, goal) pair. Since the layout is fixed and there will be hundreds of queries, PRM's amortized-cost model fits better: pay once, then answer every query with a cheap graph search.
